data.content_ref: inline:SRC_002 proposes a weight-perturbation test as the within-evaluation evidence distinguishing genuine reliability gain from mere checklist compliance. For tasks with objectively verifiable outcomes, the discriminating failure mode is compliance that tracks the right answer without tracking the underlying rationale — including cases where perturbing weights leaves the answer correct. A panel may use a checklist in a rote, surface way yet still mark the right box whenever the perturbation preserves the outcome mapping; the perturbation test only flags fragility, not compliance. By its own countercondition, the test further risks confounding fragility with incoherence when perturbation destroys the checklist. This leaves a class of compliant-but-correctly-tracking panels indistinguishable from genuinely-reliable panels under the proposed evidence, so the target does not actually satisfy the problem's demand to identify evidence that distinguishes the two.
